passage:
In the office canteen, Dilnaz pushes her lunch box away. 'Six months married, and I haven't had one cup of morning tea in peace,' she tells Vaibhav from accounts. 'Up at five for the family breakfast, home by six for dinner. My mother-in-law says the last bahu gave up her job, so why can't I cut my hours?'
'Do you want to?'
'No. I miss my mother's kitchen, my own routine, everything. But I love this work.'
Her phone buzzes. A message from her husband, Zaid: 'Talked to Ammi. From Monday I cook dinner three nights, so you don't have to rush. And she wants to hear what you think, on Sunday.'
Dilnaz reads it twice and lets out a long breath.

qa.q: By what time does Dilnaz have to be home for dinner?
qa.a: By six.

qa.q: What is Dilnaz feeling as she pushes her lunch box away?
qa.a: She feels worn out and homesick, missing her mother's kitchen and her own routine, and worried about being pushed to cut her work hours.

qa.q: What in Zaid's message could help Dilnaz settle in, and why?
qa.a: He is taking on three dinners and his mother wants to hear Dilnaz's view on Sunday, which shares the work fairly and gives her a voice.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz's mother-in-law see things differently after listening on Sunday?
qa.a: She may realise the job matters deeply to Dilnaz and that what the last bahu did need not be the rule, which could ease the tension.

grounding: Shows a new wife living with her in-laws who has lost her routines, feels pressure over her job and misses her own family, and whose adjustment eases when duties are shared and her voice is invited.

passage:
Dear Ayesha Didi,
It's 11 pm and this is my first quiet minute today. In this house breakfast is at seven sharp, the TV is always on, and I share one wardrobe mirror with three people. I've stopped my evening runs because nobody here goes out after dark, and Mummyji looked surprised when I mentioned my design deadlines. I miss our messy Sunday mornings at home so much.
But one good thing. Last night Rohit said at dinner that we'd take turns with the cooking, and his father agreed. Then Mummyji asked me which days suited me. It's the first time anyone here has asked.
Your little sister,
Ira

qa.q: What time is breakfast in Ira's new home?
qa.a: At seven sharp.

qa.q: What is Ira feeling while writing at 11 pm?
qa.a: Ira feels homesick and a little lost, missing the messy Sunday mornings at home and having given up the evening runs.

qa.q: What changed things for Ira, and why did it help?
qa.a: Rohit suggested taking turns with the cooking and Mummyji asked which days suited Ira; sharing the work and asking her opinion made her feel heard.

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Ayesha may feel worried about her little sister's loneliness but relieved by the good news at the end, and may want to call soon.

grounding: Illustrates a new wife in her in-laws' home who has given up routines and privacy and misses her own family, and who feels better once duties are shared and her opinion is asked.

passage:
12 March, night.

Day forty as the bahu of this house in Madurai. I miss my morning walk; here the kitchen starts at 5:30, and Athai likes the kolam done before the milk comes. I used to teach at a school in Coimbatore. Today I saw my old class photo on a friend's status and had to sit in the bathroom for a while.

I called Amma. She asked if I'm eating. I said yes. I didn't say I haven't read one page of my book in forty days.

Tonight something changed, a little. At dinner I finally said it: "Can the mornings be shared? I'd like one hour for myself before I start." Silence. Then Kishore said, "I'll do the milk and the kolam on alternate days." Athai looked surprised, but she nodded.

One hour. It feels enormous.

Nirmala

qa.q: When does the kitchen start in this house?
qa.a: Here the kitchen starts at 5:30.

qa.q: How is Nirmala feeling about her new life, and what shows it?
qa.a: Nirmala feels homesick and a little lost: she misses her walk and her teaching, sits in the bathroom after seeing the class photo, and hides her sadness from Amma.

qa.q: Which step helped Nirmala, and why?
qa.a: Saying plainly at dinner that she wanted the mornings shared and one hour for herself; once her voice was heard, Kishore took on alternate days.

qa.q: How might Athai see Nirmala's request?
qa.a: Athai looked surprised, perhaps expecting the new bahu to fit the house's routine, but she agreed, which suggests she can adjust.

grounding: Shows a new wife in her in-laws' home giving up routines and her teaching, missing her own family, and finding relief once duties are shared and her voice is heard.

passage:
Raksha Bandhan morning in the village near Ballia, and Pooja was up at four, grinding masala for twenty guests coming to her in-laws' house. Her own brothers, three hours away in Patna, would be waiting with empty wrists.

She hadn't asked to go. New brides didn't, here.

At the well she wiped her eyes on her dupatta before anyone could see. Vishal saw anyway.

At breakfast he spoke to his mother. "Amma, Pooja hasn't gone home in five months. I'll help Bhabhi with the cooking. Let her take the ten o'clock bus."

His mother frowned at the pot, then at Pooja. "Do you want to go?"

It was the first time anyone had asked. Pooja's voice came out small. "Yes."

"Then go. And bring back some of your mother's pickle."

qa.q: How far away are Pooja's brothers?
qa.a: Her own brothers are three hours away in Patna.

qa.q: Why did Pooja wipe her eyes at the well?
qa.a: Pooja was homesick and sad, missing her brothers on Raksha Bandhan while cooking for twenty guests at her in-laws' house.

qa.q: What made the difference for Pooja that morning?
qa.a: Vishal noticed, offered to share the cooking, and his mother asked Pooja what she wanted, so her wish finally counted.

qa.q: What might Vishal's mother have been thinking when she asked 'Do you want to go?'
qa.a: She may have been weighing the day's work against Pooja's homesickness, and realised no one had asked the new bride what she wanted.

grounding: Shows a new bride in her in-laws' village home missing her own family on a festival, and how shared duties and being asked let her go home.

passage:
Six months after the wedding, Mei, twenty-five, still woke at six in her in-laws' house in Puebla, though at home in Vancouver she used to run before work. Here, breakfast for seven came first. Her suegra, Doña Carmen, was kind but everything was done her way: the beans, the laundry, which cousin to visit on Sundays. Mei had paused her design job to "settle in". At night she video-called her mother in Cantonese, whispering so no one would think she was complaining.
One Sunday, Alejandro found her crying in the car. "I miss my own life," she said. He was quiet, then went inside and asked his mother and sisters to sit down. They made a list: breakfast on rotation, Alejandro doing laundry, Mei's mornings free for work three days a week. Doña Carmen looked hurt, then nodded. "You should have said, mija." Mei ran the next morning, lungs burning, happy.

qa.q: Where did Mei live before the wedding?
qa.a: In Vancouver.

qa.q: How was Mei feeling when Alejandro found her in the car?
qa.a: She felt homesick and lost, crying because she missed her own life, family and routines.

qa.q: What changed things, and why did it work?
qa.a: Alejandro brought the family together to share duties fairly and give Mei time for her work, so her voice was finally heard.

qa.q: How might Doña Carmen have felt when the list was made?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt at first, thinking she had been doing her best, and then understanding, saying Mei should have spoken up.

grounding: It illustrates a new wife living with in-laws who gives up routines and career and misses her family, and how fair duties and being heard help.
